stem: Which section of a business plan is usually written **last** and gives a one-page summary of the whole plan?

options.content: The executive summary
options.rationale: Correct: it summarises the finished plan, so it is written last.

options.content: The marketing plan
options.rationale: The marketing plan is a full section, not a summary of the whole.

options.content: The human resources plan
options.rationale: This section covers staff, not the whole plan.

options.content: The cash flow forecast
options.rationale: The forecast is part of the financial section.

explanation: The executive summary condenses the whole plan and is written once the other sections are complete.

stem: Which is a main purpose of a business plan?

options.content: To help persuade lenders to provide finance
options.rationale: Correct: lenders and investors expect a plan before committing money.

options.content: To guarantee that the business will make a profit
options.rationale: A plan is a forecast and guarantees nothing.

options.content: To replace the need for market research
options.rationale: A plan uses research; it does not replace it.

options.content: To avoid paying tax on early profits
options.rationale: A plan has no effect on tax.

explanation: A plan guides the owner, sets targets and helps to raise finance.

stem: A bank manager reads a start-up's business plan. What is she **most** likely to look for in the financial section?

options.content: The colour of the logo on the cover
options.rationale: Appearance does not show the ability to repay.

options.content: Evidence that the loan can be repaid
options.rationale: Correct: a lender's main concern is getting its money back with interest.

options.content: The number of friends the owner has
options.rationale: A bank lends against repayment ability and security, not friends.

options.content: Whether the owner enjoys the work
options.rationale: Enjoyment does not repay a loan.

explanation: Banks look for realistic forecasts and ability to repay.

stem: Which of the following is a **limitation** of a business plan?

options.content: It prevents the owner from borrowing money
options.rationale: A plan normally helps borrowing.

options.content: Forecasts in it may turn out to be wrong
options.rationale: Correct: figures for a new business are estimates and may be inaccurate.

options.content: It removes the need to set targets
options.rationale: Targets are part of the plan.

options.content: It cannot contain any financial information
options.rationale: The financial plan is a main section.

explanation: Plans rely on forecasts, which can be wrong, and they can go out of date.

stem: A fictional fish-farming project in Kariba lists these start-up costs: ponds US\$6,200, nets and pumps US\$3,400, first stock of fingerlings US\$1,850, licences US\$420 and working capital US\$2,130. The owner can contribute US\$4,500. How much must be borrowed?

options.rationale: This is the total funding required, before the owner's contribution.
This leaves out working capital and the contribution is also applied wrongly.
This is the owner's own contribution, not the amount to borrow.

explanation: Total funding US\$14,000 less US\$4,500 from the owner leaves US\$9,500 to borrow.
hints: Add all the costs, then subtract the owner's contribution.

stem: A supplier is deciding whether to sell timber on 60 days' credit to a new furniture maker. Which part of the maker's business plan would help the supplier **most**?

options.content: The description of the logo
options.rationale: A logo says nothing about payment.

options.content: The list of the owner's hobbies
options.rationale: Hobbies do not show ability to pay.

options.content: The cash flow forecast
options.rationale: Correct: it shows whether the maker will have cash to pay when the bill falls due.

options.content: The marketing slogan
options.rationale: A slogan does not show cash for payment.

explanation: The supplier needs to be sure of payment; the cash flow forecast shows the timing of cash in and out.
hints: What does the supplier need to know?

stem: A fictional restaurant owner in Masvingo prepares a plan using forecasts made before a large rise in fuel prices. Which is the most likely result?

options.content: The plan becomes more accurate with time
options.rationale: Plans lose accuracy when conditions change.

options.content: The plan can no longer be used by lenders in any case
options.rationale: A lender can still use it if it is updated.

options.content: The plan has no effect on future decisions
options.rationale: A plan guides later decisions, so out-of-date figures could mislead.

options.content: The plan's cost forecasts may now be wrong
options.rationale: Correct: plans become out of date when conditions change.

explanation: Forecasts are based on conditions at the time. A plan should be reviewed and updated when conditions change.
hints: Think about what happens to the cost figures.

stem: A fictional stallholder who needs no loan asks whether a 25-page formal business plan is worth the time. Which reply is the best judgement?

options.content: A plan is never worthwhile for a stall
options.rationale: Even a short plan helps to set targets and spot problems.

options.content: A longer plan is always better than a short one
options.rationale: A longer plan costs more time and is not always more useful.

options.content: A short plan is worthwhile, but a long one may not be
options.rationale: Correct: planning helps, but its value must be set against its cost.

options.content: A plan is only needed once the business fails
options.rationale: The plan is most useful before money is spent.

explanation: The benefit of planning is real, but a small business with no borrowing may need only a short plan.
hints: Weigh the benefit of planning against the cost for a small firm.

stem: A bank is more likely to lend to a new business if it can see a realistic business plan.
explanation: True. The plan shows the lender how the business will operate and how the loan will be repaid.

stem: Once a business plan has been written, it should not be changed.
explanation: False. A plan should be reviewed and revised as conditions change and results are compared with targets.

stem: Match each reader of a business plan to what they are most likely to look for.

right.content: Evidence that bills will be paid on time
A clear direction and targets to measure progress
Ability to repay the loan and security
Return on the money invested and growth prospects

explanation: Each reader uses the plan for a different purpose.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: The {{blank:a}} summary is written last, while the {{blank:b}} plan includes start-up costs and the cash flow forecast.

explanation: The executive summary is written last; the financial plan contains the costs and forecasts.

stem: The plan for a fictional sandal workshop in Bulawayo shows a selling price of US\$12 a pair, variable cost of US\$7.50 a pair and fixed costs of US\$2,700 a month. Calculate the break-even output in pairs a month.
explanation: Contribution = 12 − 7.50 = 4.50. Break-even = 2,700 ÷ 4.50 = 600 pairs. Dividing by the price (225 pairs) or by the variable cost (360 pairs) are common errors.
workedSolution: 1. Contribution = 12 − 7.50 = 4.50. Break-even = 2,700 ÷ 4.50 = 600 pairs. Dividing by the price (225 pairs) or by the variable cost (360 pairs) are common errors.
hints: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.

stem: The plan for a fictional leather-bag maker in Harare shows a selling price of US\$15 a bag, variable cost of US\$9.50 a bag and fixed costs of US\$3,300 a month. Forecast sales are 800 bags a month. Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of forecast sales, to one decimal place.
explanation: Contribution = 15 - 9.50 = 5.50; break-even = 3,300 / 5.50 = 600 bags. Margin of safety = 800 - 600 = 200 bags. 200 / 800 x 100 = 25.0%. Dividing by break-even output gives 33.3%, which is a different measure.
workedSolution: 1. Contribution = 15 - 9.50 = 5.50; break-even = 3,300 / 5.50 = 600 bags. Margin of safety = 800 - 600 = 200 bags. 200 / 800 x 100 = 25.0%. Dividing by break-even output gives 33.3%, which is a different measure.
hints: Margin of safety = forecast sales - break-even sales; divide by forecast sales.

stem: A planning forecast for a fictional juice stall in Gweru shows sales of 620 bottles in the first month (selling price US\$8, variable cost US\$5, fixed costs US\$1,500). Calculate the profit for the month.
explanation: Contribution = 620 x 3 = 1,860. Profit = 1,860 - 1,500 = US\$360. Using sales revenue less fixed costs gives US\$3,460, which ignores variable costs.
workedSolution: 1. Contribution = 620 x 3 = 1,860. Profit = 1,860 - 1,500 = US\$360. Using sales revenue less fixed costs gives US\$3,460, which ignores variable costs.

stem: State **one** element that a business plan normally contains.
explanation: Accept any element: executive summary, description and objectives, products, market analysis, marketing plan, operations, human resources or financial plan.

stem: Explain **why** a bank usually asks for a business plan before lending to a new business.

points.description: A new business has no track record, so the bank has no past accounts to judge it by
The plan shows how the business will operate and make money
The forecasts show whether the loan can be repaid, which reduces the bank's risk

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A new business has no past accounts, so the bank cannot judge it from history. The plan shows how the business will operate and earn income, and the cash flow forecast shows whether it can repay the loan. This reduces the bank's risk of not being repaid.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: What does the bank not know about a new business?

stem: Chipo plans to open a mobile phone repair shop in Masvingo. Explain **two** benefits to her of preparing a business plan.

points.description: It helps her to raise finance, as lenders expect a plan
Application: she can show a lender her expected repair numbers and costs
It shows weaknesses before money is spent
Application: she may find that the rent of a shop is too high for expected repairs

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A plan helps her to raise finance because a lender will want to see the expected number of repairs and costs. It also shows weaknesses before money is spent, for example if the plan shows the rent is too high for the number of repairs she expects.

explanation: Two benefits, each applied to the shop.
hints: Link each benefit to the repair shop.

stem: Assess whether a business plan is worth the time and cost for a very small business.

points.description: Benefit: it helps to raise finance and to set targets
Limitation: it takes time, and forecasts may be guesses
Counter-argument: a short plan costs little and may prevent an expensive mistake
Judgement with reason, e.g. worthwhile if borrowing or risk is significant

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A plan helps a small business raise finance and set targets, but it takes time and its forecasts may be wrong. A short plan costs little and can prevent an expensive mistake. It is worth the effort if the owner is borrowing or committing a large share of savings, but less so for a tiny, low-risk venture.

explanation: Both sides and a conditional judgement.
hints: Weigh benefit against cost and finish with a condition.

stem: Outline **three** steps in preparing a business plan.

points.description: Identify the opportunity and set objectives
Research the market, costs and competitors
Work out the funding required and expected profit, then write and review the plan

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: First identify the opportunity and set objectives. Then research the market, the costs and competitors. Finally work out the funding and expected profit, then write the plan and have it checked.

explanation: Any three correct steps.
hints: Think of the order: idea, research, figures, writing.

stem:
A fictional business: Sipho plans a small bakery in Mutare. His plan shows the start-up costs below, a selling price of US\$3.20 per loaf of premium bread, variable cost of US\$1.70 per loaf and fixed costs of US\$1,050 a month.

| Start-up item | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Oven and tins | 5,200 |
| Shop fittings | 2,750 |
| First stock of flour and packaging | 1,480 |
| Licences | 260 |
| Working capital | 910 |

Sipho can contribute US\$4,000 of his own money.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount Sipho needs to borrow.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the break-even output in loaves a month.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** pieces of information a bank would look for in the plan.

points.description: Evidence of how the loan will be repaid (cash flow forecast)
Evidence of demand for the product or security offered

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The bank would look for a cash flow forecast showing how the loan will be repaid, and evidence that customers will buy the bread.

explanation: Loan US\$6,600; break-even 700 loaves; a lender wants repayment evidence and demand evidence.

stem: A fictional business: Rudo has prepared a plan for an internet café in Gweru. Her forecasts assume 60 customers a day, but she based this on one week of counting passers-by in the month when a trade fair was held nearby. A potential investor says the plan is too optimistic.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain **one** weakness in the way Rudo prepared her forecast.

points.description: She used a single week of data
The week was unusual because of the trade fair
So her forecast of 60 customers may overstate normal demand

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She used only one week of passers-by, and that week was unusual because of the trade fair, so her forecast of 60 customers a day may be much higher than normal demand.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Rudo should revise her plan before approaching lenders.

points.description: Benefit: a realistic plan is more credible to lenders
Benefit: lower forecasts allow her to see whether the café can still break even
Cost: research takes time and delays the start
Risk of not revising: borrowing too much or losing credibility if sales are lower
Counter-argument: she could present best and worst cases
Judgement and reason

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A realistic plan is more credible to lenders and shows whether the café could still break even on lower demand. Revising costs time and delays the opening, but lending on over-optimistic figures could lead to repayment problems and loss of credibility. She could present best-case and worst-case forecasts. On balance she should collect data over several ordinary weeks first, because a plan that the lender trusts is worth the short delay.

parts.explanation: Both sides, then a reasoned decision.
hints: Compare the cost of delay with the risk of an over-optimistic plan.

explanation: A single unusual week is weak evidence; a revised plan is more credible.
hints: Think about what makes a forecast reliable.
